geo.title: What to know
geo.body:
Card sort: evidence vs. counterexample vs. proof.

Goal: I can connect evidence, counterexample, and proof.

  • 1.1 I can explain why we question what our eyes tell us.
  • 1.2 I can make a conjecture from a pattern and test it.
  • 1.3 I can use points, lines, and planes to describe a map.
  • 1.4 I can name and measure angles and describe how Eratosthenes used them.
  • 1.5 I can classify polygons and see patterns in repeated shapes.
  • 1.6 I can copy a segment and draw a circle with compass and straightedge.
  • 1.7 I can explain why geometry needs undefined terms and postulates.
  • 1.8 I can write a conditional, its converse, inverse, and contrapositive.
  • 1.9 I can test whether a definition is a good one by checking both directions.
  • 1.10 I can write a short chain of reasoning in paragraph and two-column form.
  • 1.11 I can prove a statement by showing its opposite leads to a contradiction.
  • 1.12 I can tell the difference between postulates, definitions, and theorems.

slides.title: Practice: 1.1
slides.html: A drawing shows two angles that look equal. Is that enough to say they are equal?
slides.reveal: No. A drawing can suggest a conjecture, but only measurement within a stated error or, better, a proof can settle it. In geometry we prove it.

geo.body:

From lesson 1.1, Euclid, the Surfer, and the Spotter.

slides.title: Practice: 1.4
slides.html: If two cities are 800 km apart and the angle is 7.2 degrees, about how big is Earth's circumference?
slides.reveal: 7.2 degrees is 1/50 of 360 degrees, so about 50 times 800 km = 40,000 km.

geo.title: Practice: 1.4
geo.body:
If two cities are 800 km apart and the angle is 7.2 degrees, about how big is Earth's circumference?

From lesson 1.4, Angles and Measuring the Earth.

slides.title: Practice: 1.7
slides.html: Why can't every word in geometry be defined?
slides.reveal: Each definition uses other words, so defining everything would be circular or go on forever. We must start with some undefined terms.

geo.title: Practice: 1.7
geo.body:
Why can't every word in geometry be defined?

From lesson 1.7, We Can't Go On Like This.

slides.title: Practice: 1.10
slides.html: In a two-column proof, what must every statement have next to it?
slides.reveal: A reason: given, a definition, a postulate, a property, or a theorem already proved.

slides.title: Common traps
slides.html:
Watch out for these common mistakes:

  • a few examples prove a rule
  • a drawing that looks right is right
  • converse of a true statement is automatically true
  • definitions are "just vocabulary" rather than reversible statements
